lesson.title: Reading the Sign Change: The First Derivative Test
lesson.summary: The First Derivative Test classifies each critical number by checking how the sign of the derivative behaves on either side of it: positive to negative signals a local maximum, negative to positive signals a local minimum, and no change signals neither.
lesson.body:
Let c be a critical number of f, with f continuous at c. Examine the sign of f'(x), positive or negative, on an interval immediately to the left of c and on an interval immediately to the right of c, staying inside the domain and not crossing any other critical number along the way. The First Derivative Test reads off the classification directly from that pattern. If f' is positive just to the left of c and negative just to the right, f has a local maximum at c. If f' is negative just to the left of c and positive just to the right, f has a local minimum at c. If f' has the same sign on both sides, positive on both sides or negative on both sides, then f has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum at c.

The reasoning behind the test is exactly the rising and falling intuition from earlier sections, now made precise. A positive derivative means the function is increasing, a negative derivative means it is decreasing. Increasing then decreasing traces out a peak, a local maximum. Decreasing then increasing traces out a valley, a local minimum. Increasing on both sides, or decreasing on both sides, means the function paused for an instant, perhaps flattening its tangent or hitting a corner, but kept heading in the same overall direction, so there was no peak or valley there at all, exactly the situation seen already with x^3 at x = 0 and with x^(1/3) at x = 0.

Apply the test to the polynomial from the critical number section, f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 5, whose critical numbers were found to be x = -1 and x = 2, with f'(x) = 6(x - 2)(x + 1). These two critical numbers split the real line into three intervals: (-infinity, -1), (-1, 2), and (2, infinity). Pick one convenient test point inside each interval and check the sign of f' there. In (-infinity, -1), try x = -2: f'(-2) = 6(-2 - 2)(-2 + 1) = 6(-4)(-1) = 24, which is positive. In (-1, 2), try x = 0: f'(0) = 6(0 - 2)(0 + 1) = 6(-2)(1) = -12, which is negative. In (2, infinity), try x = 3: f'(3) = 6(3 - 2)(3 + 1) = 6(1)(4) = 24, which is positive.

So the sign pattern reads positive, then negative, then positive, moving left to right. At x = -1, the sign changes from positive to negative, so f has a local maximum at x = -1, with local maximum value f(-1) = 12, matching the value computed earlier. At x = 2, the sign changes from negative to positive, so f has a local minimum at x = 2, with local minimum value f(2) = -15.

Organizing critical numbers, test points, and the resulting plus and minus signs along a single number line, exactly the way the last paragraph laid it out, is such a useful habit that it earns its own name: a sign chart. The next section turns this bookkeeping into an explicit, repeatable tool, especially valuable once a function has more than two critical numbers to track at once.
